title: Normalization branches at a nodal contraction boundary
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], $X,Y$ proper reduced $k$-schemes of pure dimension one [def-weil-proper-morphism, def-pc-reduced-scheme, def-weil-pure-dimension], and $f:Y\to X$ a proper surjective $k$-morphism. Let $x\in X(k)$ be a closed point, let $Z=Y\times_X\operatorname{Spec}k$ be its scheme-theoretic fibre [def-pc-scheme-fibre], and let $B=Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ have its reduced induced closed subscheme structure [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]. Assume $B$ is nonempty, connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] and pure of dimension one, $Y\setminus B\to X\setminus\{x\}$ is an isomorphism, and an open neighbourhood of $B$ in $Y$ is nodal: every nonsmooth closed point [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] has completed local ring $k[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion, def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Then the reduced irreducible components of $Y$ not contained in $B$ correspond bijectively to the irreducible components of $X$, and their smooth proper normalizations [def-sc-normalization] are identified over $X$ by $f$. Under these identifications the normalization of $X$ maps to $Y$ and identifies the set of points over $x$ bijectively with the boundary $B\cap\overline{Y\setminus B}$. In particular that boundary is nonempty. Each such point is a node of $Y$ with exactly one branch in $B$ and one branch outside $B$. If $x$ is an ordinary $n$-fold point, meaning
$$\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X,x}\cong k[[t_1,\ldots,t_n]]/(t_it_j\mid i\ne j),\qquad n\ge1,$$
then the scheme-theoretic fibre $Z$ is reduced, hence $Z=B$. No equality of arithmetic genera, rationality of contracted components, tree condition, or marking hypothesis is assumed.

source.place: Appendix B, Corollary B.2 proof, last paragraph on normalization and boundary, printed p. 58; reduced-fibre clause is the local ordinary-branch calculation made explicit (agent refinement). Primary PDF read online; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Properness over $k$ includes finite type, so [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] makes $X,Y$ Noetherian (a field has only the ideals $0,k$). Put $A=\overline{Y\setminus B}_{\mathrm{red}}$. Apply [lem-trf-complementary-pure-subcurve-components] to $B\subset Y$: $B$ is a union of whole reduced components and $A$ is the union of all the others. Apply [lem-trf-nodal-subcurve-boundary] to the same inclusion, using the stipulated nodal neighbourhood. It gives $T=A\cap B=\coprod_{j=1}^r\operatorname{Spec}k$, possibly empty at this stage; each point of $T$ is an ambient node and is smooth on both $A$ and $B$. In the completed node ring the two reduced subcurves are the two distinct axes: both are smooth and their union is the whole node, so neither can contain both minimal primes. Thus one branch is in $B$ and the other in $A$.

The open $X\setminus\{x\}$ contains every generic point of $X$, since all components have dimension one. The open $Y\setminus B$ contains exactly the generic points of the components of $A$. An isomorphism of these opens identifies their generic points, and taking closures gives the asserted component bijection. A reduced component $A_i$ maps into its corresponding reduced component $X_i$: locally the ideal of $X_i$ pulls back to functions vanishing at every point of $A_i$, hence to zero because $A_i$ is reduced. The generic-point identification identifies their function fields. No component of $A$ is contracted.

source.place: Appendix B, Corollary B.2 proof, final normalization paragraph, p. 58; generic-point argument expanded.

proof.text: The restriction $A_i\to X_i$ is proper. Indeed $A_i\to Y\to X$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](a),(c); as it factors through the closed immersion $X_i\hookrightarrow X$, its factor is the base change of this proper map along $X_i\hookrightarrow X$. Its fibres away from $x$ have at most one point, and its fibre at $x$ is contained in the finite set $T$. By [thm-pqf-finite-iff-proper-finite-fibres] it is finite. Use [lem-sc-normalization-properties] on $A_i$ and $X_i$: their normalizations are finite, surjective, birational and proper, and are smooth since the algebraically closed field is perfect. By [lem-sc-smooth-normal] the normalized source is normal. The dominant composite $\widetilde A_i\to X_i$ therefore lifts to $p_i:\widetilde A_i\to\widetilde X_i$ by [lem-sbc-normalization-dominant-lift].

source.place: Tag 035Q (lemma-normalization), universal property (4); Cohomology of Schemes, Tag 02OG (lemma-characterize-finite).

proof.text: The map $p_i$ is finite: over an affine $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset X_i$, write the two finite inverse images as $\operatorname{Spec}C=\widetilde X_i|_U$ and $\operatorname{Spec}D=\widetilde A_i|_U$. Here $D$ is finite over $R$ because both $\widetilde A_i\to A_i$ and $A_i\to X_i$ are finite; explicitly products of finite module generators generate their composite. The same $R$-module generators of $D$ generate it as a $C$-module. Localizing at any element of $C$ proves finiteness over the principal affine opens of $\operatorname{Spec}C$. The common function field in Step 2 makes $p_i$ birational. Its target is normal by smoothness and [lem-sc-smooth-normal], so [lem-trf-finite-birational-normal-iso] makes $p_i$ an isomorphism. Taking the disjoint union of the inverse isomorphisms and composing with $\widetilde A_i\to A_i\hookrightarrow Y$ constructs $h:\widetilde X\to Y$ over $X$.

source.place: Tag 0AB1 (lemma-finite-birational-over-normal); affine finite-module calculation for the lifted map.

proof.text: The points of $h(\nu_X^{-1}(x))$ are exactly $A\cap B$: $h$ is surjective onto $A$ component by component, and the underlying fibre of $f$ is $|B|$. At any $y\in T$, $A$ is smooth by Step 1, hence normal by [lem-sc-smooth-normal] applied to a smooth open neighbourhood in $A$. The normalization is an isomorphism there by [lem-sc-normalization-properties](b). Thus exactly one point of the disjoint union $\coprod_i\widetilde A_i$ maps to $y$ (smoothness also prevents distinct components of $A$ meeting there). This proves bijectivity. At least one component $X_i$ passes through $x$; surjectivity of its normalization from [lem-sc-normalization-properties](a) supplies a point over $x$. Hence $T$ is nonempty. Together with Step 1 this proves every assertion except the final scheme-fibre clause.

source.place: Appendix B, Corollary B.2 proof, final paragraph, p. 58; boundary smoothness supplied by Stacks 0E38.

proof.text: Now suppose $x$ is ordinary. Write $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_{X,x}$, and $S$ for its integral closure in its total ring of fractions, namely the semilocal ring of $\widetilde X$ above $x$. Here $R$ is reduced and essentially of finite type over $k$. Its dimension is one: prime chains in a local affine chart have length at most one, and a component generic point specializing to the closed nongeneric $x$ gives length one. By [lem-trf-curve-normalization-completion], $S$ is finite over $R$ and $S\otimes_R\widehat R$ is the integral closure of $\widehat R$. In the given ordinary model, restriction to each axis identifies $\widehat R$ with the ring of tuples $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\prod_i k[[t_i]]$ having equal constant coefficients. Its integral closure is $P=\prod_i k[[t_i]]$: adjoining the coordinate idempotents (each satisfying $e_i^2=e_i$) gives $P$, and a tuple integral in $\prod_i k((t_i))$ has no negative order in any coordinate. Indeed in a monic equation a negative-order leading power has strictly smaller order than every other term and cannot cancel. This also proves each $k[[t_i]]$ integrally closed directly. The total fraction ring is the displayed product of Laurent fields: invert the non-zero-divisor $(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$ to separate axes and invert their parameters. Hence $\mathfrak mP=\prod_i(t_i)$ and $P/\mathfrak mP=k^n$.

source.place: Equation (multicross) in Section multicross, before Tag 0C1V; varieties.tex Tag 0C3V (lemma-normalization-same-after-completion).

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat], $R\to\widehat R$ is faithfully flat. Thus $S/\mathfrak mS$ injects into $(S/\mathfrak mS)\otimes_R\widehat R=P/\mathfrak mP=k^n$, and is reduced. To spell out the injectivity used here, for any module element $z$, tensor the inclusion of its cyclic submodule with the flat algebra; if $z\otimes1=0$ that entire tensor module vanishes, and faithfulness forces the cyclic submodule to vanish. Localizing $S/\mathfrak mS$ at a point $q$ above $x$ gives a reduced finite-dimensional local $k$-algebra. Its only prime is its maximal ideal (a finite-dimensional domain quotient is a field), so that ideal, being the nilradical, is zero. Consequently $\mathfrak mS_q$ is the maximal ideal of $S_q$. Under Steps 4 and 5, $S_q=\mathcal O_{A,y}$ for the corresponding boundary point $y$. Therefore the image of $\mathfrak m$ generates the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{A,y}$.

source.place: Tag 00MC (lemma-completion-faithfully-flat); descent and localization argument written explicitly.

proof.text: Fix such a boundary point $y$, put $H=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ and $J=\mathfrak mH$, the ideal of the scheme-theoretic fibre. Its restriction to $\mathcal O_{B,y}$ is zero: the composite $B\to X$ factors through $x$, since the maximal ideal pulls back to functions vanishing at all points of the reduced $B$. In $\widehat H=k[[u,v]]/(uv)$ label the axes so that $A$ is $v=0$ and $B$ is $u=0$. Completion preserves the defining quotient sequences by [lem-weil-pbc-completion-exact-finite-modules]; thus $J\widehat H\subseteq(u)$. Step 7 says its image on the $A$-axis generates that axis's maximal ideal. Choose a finite linear combination of generators of $J$ whose restriction is a generator there. Its completed image is $u a(u)$ with $a(0)\ne0$, hence it generates $(u)$ in $\widehat H$. It follows that $J\widehat H=(u)$ and $\widehat H/J\widehat H=k[[v]]$, a domain (the lowest nonzero coefficients of a product multiply). Faithful flatness of $H\to\widehat H$ from [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat] embeds $H/J$ into this domain, by the cyclic-module argument of Step 7. Thus $H/J$ is reduced.

source.place: Tags 00MB (lemma-completion-flat, exactness on finite modules) and 00MC; explicit node-axis calculation.

proof.text: On $Y\setminus A$ the whole reduced scheme is an open subscheme of $B$, since $A,B$ are the complementary unions of components. The pullback of $\mathfrak m$ is zero there by reducedness, as in Step 8; hence $Z$ is reduced there. Its remaining points lie in $A\cap B=T$, where Step 8 proves reducedness of every fibre local ring. There are no points of $Z$ outside $B$. Reducedness is the absence of nilpotents in local rings, so $Z$ is reduced everywhere. Its support is $|B|$, and the unique reduced induced closed subscheme on that support is $B$ by [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]; therefore $Z=B$. This used neither genus equality nor any rationality, graph, or marking condition.

source.place: Ordinary-branch local calculation after Equation (multicross), together with the node-axis calculation above; final reduced-structure identification.
